meta.descriptionEn: On 29 October 2018, a nearly new Boeing 737 MAX 8 took off from Jakarta on a short domestic flight. Eleven minutes later it was gone. What happened in those minutes would ground an entire fleet of aircraft around the world. This documentary follows the story of Lion Air Flight 610: the crew's struggle, the search in the Java Sea, and the investigation that uncovered a hidden software system called MCAS, a single sensor, a miscalibrated part, and a chain of decisions made years earlier. We look at what Boeing, the FAA, the airline and maintenance teams got wrong, how a second crash in Ethiopia followed, and what has changed for aviation safety since. Based only on official reports and documented sources.
meta.descriptionUr: 29 October 2018 ko Jakarta se aik bilkul nayi Boeing 737 MAX 8 ne udaan bhari, aur sirf 11 minute baad woh samandar mein gir gayi. Is documentary mein hum Lion Air Flight 610 ki poori kahani dekhte hain: pilots ki jaddo-jehad, Java Sea mein talaash, aur woh tehqeeq jis ne MCAS naam ke chupe huay software, aik hi sensor aur kharab maintenance ka raaz khola. Phir Ethiopia ka doosra hadsa aur poori dunya mein 737 MAX ki grounding. Hum jaanenge ke kya galat hua aur hum ne kya seekha. Video aakhir tak zaroor dekhein.

articleEn: On the morning of 29 October 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 was getting ready to leave Jakarta's Soekarno–Hatta airport. The aircraft took off at 6:20 a.m., bound for Depati Amir Airport in Pangkal Pinang, where it was due to land at 7:20. But just three minutes later, the captain asked the controller for permission to return to the airport because of flight-control problems. At 6:33, air traffic control lost contact. The jet had fallen into the Java Sea, only 11 minutes after takeoff. All 189 people on board lost their lives. We remember them with respect and will tell their story with care.

An offshore oil platform was nearby. According to reports, workers there saw the aircraft plunge into the sea at a very steep nose-down angle. It was a brand-new aircraft, a Boeing 737 MAX 8. So the question is: why did a new jet go down so fast, and why did the pilots not know what was happening? According to investigations, Boeing had deliberately kept a software function, MCAS, out of the pilots' documentation.

The biggest question comes last: how did this one accident eventually lead to the grounding of the 737 MAX around the world? In this video we look at what MCAS was, what mistakes were made in maintenance and by the crew, and what the accident taught aviation. Let's begin.

articleEn: The aircraft flying as Lion Air Flight 610 was registered PK-LQP, a Boeing 737 MAX 8. It had been delivered to Lion Air, brand new, on 13 August 2018, and by the time of the accident it had flown about 800 hours. It was powered by two CFM International LEAP-1B engines. The 737 MAX itself was new too, having entered service on 22 May 2017.

Flight 610 was the first major accident involving this type. No 737 MAX had been a hull loss before, and it became the deadliest accident in the 737 family. It was also the deadliest in Lion Air's history; before it, Flight 538 in 2004 had killed 25 people. In Indonesia it was the deadliest aircraft accident since Garuda Indonesia Flight 152 in 1997, and the deadliest ever in the Java Sea.

Now let's step into the cockpit. Captain Bhavye Suneja was a 31-year-old Indian citizen who had worked with Lion Air for more than seven years. He had 6,028 hours of flying experience, 5,176 of them on the Boeing 737, and he had trained in California. With him was First Officer Harvino, a 41-year-old Indonesian citizen with 5,174 hours, of which 4,286 were on the 737. Both pilots were therefore well experienced on the 737, but the MAX had something new that they did not know about.

There were also six flight attendants, all Indonesian, making eight crew members in total, along with 181 passengers: 178 adults, one child and two infants. Behind every number was a person and a family.

Among the passengers were 38 government employees. They included 20 from the Ministry of Finance, 10 from the Audit Board of Indonesia and three police officers. Three public prosecutors, three judges and six members of the Bangka Belitung regional council were also on board. Two foreign nationals were aboard: Captain Bhavye Suneja himself, and Italian passenger Andrea Manfredi, a former professional cyclist.

This was a scheduled domestic flight from Jakarta's Soekarno–Hatta Airport to Depati Amir Airport in Pangkal Pinang. But problems had already appeared on this same aircraft's previous flight. First, let's understand what was actually new in the MAX.

chapters.covers: Larger LEAP-1B engines placed forward and higher causing nose-up tendency; goal of commonality with 737NG and avoiding simulator training; MCAS concept from KC-46 tanker; test pilots Ray Craig and Ed Wilson; March 2016 redesign increasing authority; reliance on a single AoA sensor; hazardous (not catastrophic) classification; three-second reaction assumption; removal of MCAS from manuals approved by FAA; later FAA/EASA view that plane might have been stable without MCAS.

articleEn: So what was new in the MAX? The story starts with its engines. The LEAP engines were larger than those on earlier 737 generations, so they had to be mounted farther forward of the wing and higher off the ground. This changed the aircraft's aerodynamics. As a result, with flaps up, at a high angle of attack and in manual flight, the aircraft's nose tended to pitch upward.

Boeing wanted the MAX to feel exactly like the older 737 Next Generation. That way both variants could share one type rating, and airlines could use the same pilots on both and save on differences training. Boeing said this meant simulator training was no longer needed.

Where did the idea of MCAS come from? According to a Wall Street Journal report, engineers who had worked on the KC-46 tanker suggested it to the design team. The KC-46 also has MCAS, but there the system shuts off when the pilot makes a stick input. The 737 MAX's MCAS did not work that way. Before MCAS, test pilot Ray Craig determined that the aircraft was not flying smoothly, partly because of the larger engines. Later, a new test pilot, Ed Wilson, said the MAX was not handling well near a stall at low speed. He recommended applying MCAS across a wider range of conditions, which meant the stabilizer had to move faster and farther.

In March 2016, Boeing's General Manager and Chief Project Engineer for the 737 MAX program approved a redesign of MCAS so that FAA stall requirements would be met. According to one report, MCAS moved the stabilizer four times more than in the initial safety analysis document. Just a few hours after the redesign was approved, Boeing asked for references to MCAS to be removed from the flight crew operations manual, and the FAA agreed. The FAA officials who gave that permission only learned after the Lion Air accident that MCAS had been redesigned.

Another major problem was that MCAS read data from only one angle-of-attack sensor, even though the aircraft has two. That was a single point of failure. The safety analysis classified MCAS failure as hazardous, meaning serious harm was possible but not catastrophic. There was one more assumption attached: the design held, and the FAA accepted, that pilots would react within three seconds to an unexpected MCAS activation. The NTSC's final report later said these assumptions about crew response, although consistent with industry guidelines, proved incorrect.

One important point: in post-accident assessments, directors at the FAA and EASA believed the aircraft would have been acceptably stable even without MCAS. So MCAS rested on three things: one sensor, hidden software and very little time. But what happened to that sensor on the Lion Air jet?

articleEn: The story of this Lion Air jet began before the crash. The first signs of trouble appeared on its last few flights. On 7 November the NTSC confirmed that AoA sensor problems had occurred on the third-to-last and fourth-to-last flights before the accident. In Bali, engineers thought replacing a sensor might fix the problem, so one of the aircraft's AoA sensors was replaced.

The replacement was a used part supplied by the American company Xtra Aerospace. Later investigation found that it was probably miscalibrated even when it was shipped. The test after installation was also questionable, and investigators could not establish that it had been done correctly.

Now to the flight that night from Denpasar to Jakarta. This was the penultimate flight, the one just before the accident flight. A few minutes after takeoff the aircraft suddenly pitched down. According to the NTSC, the crew used inflight procedures and continued the flight at a lower altitude than usual. Passengers said the cabin shook violently and smelled of burnt rubber. At one point the aircraft dropped more than 60 meters in a few seconds. According to an air traffic control recording, the pilot made a pan-pan call, which the crew later canceled before continuing to Jakarta.
After landing, the crew reported a 20-degree difference between the left and right AoA sensor readings. That was a very big warning sign.

A third pilot was also in the cockpit on this flight. News later emerged that he told the crew to cut power to the stabilizer trim motors. The NTSC confirmed an off-duty pilot's presence in the cockpit but did not confirm his role, so this part is not fully established. The procedure is a standard memory item on the 737 checklist, and on this flight it fixed the problem; in other words, the runaway stabilizer checklist worked. According to the preliminary report, the crew felt automatic nose-down trim, switched off the electric stabilizer trim, and landed with manual trim.

The real trouble began after landing. The maintenance logbook mentioned a navigation failure, but it did not mention the continuous stick shaker or the runaway stabilizer checklist. According to the NTSC, that omission meant the maintenance crew in Jakarta did not get full information, and neither did the next day's crew.

Lion Air CEO Edward Sirait said the technical issue had been resolved according to the manuals. Engineers cleared the aircraft to fly the next morning. So the jet was ready to fly again, though the question over the sensor remained and the crew knew nothing of MCAS. What happened next?

articleEn: On the morning of 29 October 2018, Flight 610 took off from Soekarno–Hatta at 6:20 a.m., bound for Pangkal Pinang, where it was due at 7:20 a.m. The aircraft first flew west, then turned to head northeast. The weather was clear with good visibility, and there were no cumulonimbus clouds.

Just three minutes later, the captain asked the controller for permission to return to the airport because of a flight-control problem. Another account says the request came after 19 nautical miles of flight. The details differ, but the problem was there from the start.

The aircraft's data now looked strange. At about 8 minutes, the jet had reached 1,500 meters, or 5,000 feet, but its altitude kept going up and down. Airspeed data was also unusual: it averaged about 300 knots, whereas below 3,000 meters the limit is normally 250 knots.

According to the preliminary report, over the last ten minutes MCAS repeatedly commanded nose-down trim because of faulty AoA data, and the crew repeatedly tried nose-up trim. The preliminary report did not say whether the runaway stabilizer procedure was run. But according to the summary of the investigation, the pilots did not follow the checklist properly. As a result, MCAS stayed active, and the aircraft repeatedly went into an unsafe nose-down position.

An important alert also stayed silent. According to the NTSC, the AoA DISAGREE alert had not been properly enabled during development. As a result, it did not show up in flight with the miscalibrated sensor, and the crew could not log it in the logbook either.

What was the situation in the cockpit? In its final report, the NTSC cited multiple alerts, repeated MCAS activations and a great deal of communication with ATC. According to the report, all of this could not be managed effectively. The reasons were the difficulty of the situation, manual handling, checklist execution and communication within the crew. The result was ineffective CRM, or crew resource management, and poor workload management. The report also says such weaknesses had already been seen during training.
But to be fair, these pilots did not know about MCAS. The NTSC also counted the lack of guidance in manuals and training as a contributing factor.

Air traffic control lost contact at 6:33 a.m. The aircraft crashed into the Java Sea, which sources put at about 11 minutes after takeoff. On 5 November the NTSC said the aircraft was roughly intact at the time of the crash and hit the sea at very high speed. The engines were also running at the time. Oil platform workers reportedly saw the aircraft falling at a steep nose-down angle. According to the head of the Police Hospital, an explosion or fire was unlikely.
The big question now was how to find the aircraft in the sea, and where were the answers locked inside the recorders?

articleEn: As soon as contact was lost, Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency, Basarnas, went into action. At first three ships and a helicopter were sent. At 7:30 a.m. the agency was informed that Flight 610 had crashed near an offshore oil platform. Boats from the platform set out, and debris was soon found.

The Indonesian Navy, Air Force and Republic of Singapore Navy also joined the search. At first about 150 people reached the site with boats and helicopters. The aircraft had come down about 34 kilometers from the Java coast, in water at most 35 meters deep. But poor visibility and strong currents made the work difficult.

Then on 1 November came a major success: the Flight 610 flight data recorder, or FDR, was found at a depth of 32 meters. It was in poor condition, and its memory unit had separated from its housing. Even so, investigators recovered data from the last 19 flights, or 69 hours. Singapore's Transport Safety Investigation Bureau sent three specialists, and two people from Australia's ATSB helped download the FDR data.

On 2 November a volunteer rescue diver died during the search, a very sad moment in the whole effort. On the same day more than 850 people and 45 vessels were involved, and the aerial search area was extended to 190 nautical miles. The landing gear and engines were also found. The main body of the aircraft was located 7.5 nautical miles from the shore at Tanjung Pakis, about 200 meters from where the FDR was found. On 4 November about 1,400 people, 175 divers and 69 ships were at the site.

On 10 November Basarnas ended the search for victims. By 23 November victim identification was complete. Of the 189 people, 125 were identified, including both foreigners, while 64 could not be identified. For relatives, Lion Air provided free flights to Jakarta, and on 30 October more than 90 relatives were brought there. Police announced a trauma-healing team, and Jasa Raharja announced 50 million rupiah for each family. Later, some families claimed they were pressured to give up their legal rights.

The biggest remaining problem was the cockpit voice recorder, or CVR. Lion Air paid US$2.8 million for a second search from 19 to 29 December. Divers picked up the beacon's signal beneath the wreckage but could not recover the CVR. The NTSC then began a new search using KRI Spica. Finally, on 14 January 2019, the CVR was found, 30 meters deep and buried under 8 meters of thick mud.
Now investigators had both recorders. Did they hold the answers the whole world was waiting for?

articleEn: On 28 November 2018 the NTSC released its preliminary accident investigation report. It covered the flights before the accident and the initial details of the accident flight. According to the report, the accident aircraft's AoA sensor had been replaced and tested two days earlier. But the 28 October flight also showed incorrect airspeed indications, and automatic nose-down trim occurred on it. The crew ran the runaway stabilizer checklist, switched off the electric trim and landed with manual trim.

On the morning of 29 October, immediately after takeoff, the same problem returned. Because of incorrect AoA data, MCAS commanded automatic nose-down trim. In the last ten minutes the flight crew repeatedly tried nose-up trim. But the preliminary report did not say whether the runaway stabilizer procedure was carried out.

Meanwhile, Boeing issued an Operations Manual Bulletin on 6 November, stating that with incorrect AoA data the stabilizer could move down for up to 10 seconds. The next day, 7 November, the FAA issued an emergency airworthiness directive, warning that this unsafe condition could lead to impact with terrain. Then on 10 November Boeing named MCAS for the first time. In other words, twelve days after the accident, the world learned that this system actually existed.

In November, Aviation Week looked at the 737 MAX flight-crew operations manual and found no mention of MCAS. Pilots at American and Southwest turned out to be unaware of it too. On 15 November the Air Line Pilots Association of America, which represents 61,000 pilots, asked the FAA to make sure pilots were given all relevant information. Boeing defended itself, saying the successful troubleshooting on 28 October proved that MCAS had not changed the runaway stabilizer procedures.

Finally, on 25 October 2019, the NTSC's final report came out. It listed nine contributing factors and did not rank them by importance. They included faulty assumptions in Boeing's design, MCAS relying on only one AoA sensor, and a lack of MCAS guidance in manuals and training. The AoA DISAGREE alert had also not been properly enabled. The replacement sensor had been miscalibrated in an earlier repair, and the installation test could not be established. According to the report, 31 pages of the logbook were missing. The failure to record the continuous stick shaker and the runaway stabilizer checklist made decisions harder for both maintenance and the crew.
The report also identified weaknesses at Lion Air, and the FAA revoked Xtra Aerospace's repair certificate, effectively ending that company's business.

In January 2020, internal Boeing messages came out. They included mockery of Lion Air's 2017 request for additional simulator training. Lion Air co-founder Rusdi Kirana, who said Boeing was putting the blame on Lion Air, considered canceling orders for 190 aircraft.

articleEn: Friends, the story did not end there. On 10 March 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed shortly after taking off from Addis Ababa. All 157 people on board died. Between the two accidents, 346 people lost their lives. According to satellite data, both aircraft struggled to gain altitude after takeoff.

On 11 March China became the first to ground the 737 MAX. The next day Indonesia, Singapore, India, Turkey, South Korea, the European Union, Australia and Malaysia did the same. The situation in America was different. On 11 March the FAA issued a Continued Airworthiness Notice, while Boeing CEO Dennis Muilenburg was calling the MAX safe. Then pressure grew, and on 13 March 2019 the FAA also ordered a grounding. According to evidence at the crash site, the stabilizer jackscrew was in a nose-down position. About 30 MAX aircraft were in American airspace at the time, and they were allowed to reach their destinations.

By 18 March, all 387 aircraft worldwide were grounded. This affected about 8,600 flights each week for 59 airlines. Some ferry flights were flown with flaps extended so that MCAS would not activate. According to Ethiopian investigators, the crew tried the recommended recovery procedure but could not recover. Another source says the pilots did not complete the checklist. Ethiopia's final report came much later, on 23 December 2022. The probable cause was MCAS's repeated uncommanded nose-down inputs, produced by faulty AoA input.

The question was how well the FAA understood the risk. According to a private analysis from December 2018, MCAS could cause 15 fatal crashes. The estimate covered a 30-year period and projected about 2,900 deaths. This study came out a year later, at a House hearing in December 2019.

On 4 April 2019, Boeing publicly acknowledged that MCAS was involved in both accidents because it acted on faulty data from one AoA sensor. Boeing also prepared a software update and cut production to 42 aircraft a month. Later, from January 2020, MAX production was temporarily halted. At a hearing on 13 May 2019, Sam Graves said that pilots trained in America would have succeeded. But later investigations raised serious questions about design and certification.

On 30 October 2019, Dennis Muilenburg appeared before congressional committees. On 26 November the FAA took back from Boeing the authority to issue airworthiness certificates. On 23 December 2019, Muilenburg was removed. David Calhoun took over as CEO in January 2020 and promised to improve safety and transparency. A House report in September 2020 held both Boeing and the FAA responsible for flaws in design and certification.
So how did the MAX come back?

articleEn: In 2020, an FAA Airworthiness Directive approved design changes for every MAX. MCAS could now activate only when both AoA sensors' readings agreed. It could not activate repeatedly, and pilots could override it when necessary. Boeing also changed the flight-control computer architecture to provide better redundancy. The FAA required special simulator training for the MAX, including recovery from a simulated MCAS failure.
On 18 November 2020, the FAA ended the grounding of about 20 months, the longest grounding of any American airliner. Indonesia lifted its ban in December 2021.

In January 2021, Boeing reached a settlement of more than 2.5 billion dollars. It included a 243.6 million criminal penalty, 1.77 billion for airlines and 500 million for the families of victims. The direct cost of the groundings is estimated at about 20 billion dollars, while indirect losses were more than 60 billion. The effect was felt across the whole industry.

So what did we learn? The first lesson is transparency: pilots must know about the systems that fly the aircraft. The second is certification: assumptions must be tested rigorously. The third is maintenance and training, because a miscalibrated sensor and incomplete logs also played a part. The fourth is practice in crew resource management and workload handling. And questions about oversight remain open: is the balance between regulators and manufacturers right?

shorts.text: صرف 11 منٹ! اتنی دیر میں ایک جہاز سمندر میں جا گرا۔ 29 اکتوبر 2018 کی صبح، Lion Air کی Flight 610 نے Jakarta سے 6:20 پر takeoff کیا۔ منزل Pangkal Pinang تھی۔ مگر صرف 3 منٹ بعد captain نے controller سے واپس airport آنے کی اجازت مانگی۔ وجہ تھی flight-control کے مسائل۔ پھر 6:33 پر air traffic control کا رابطہ ٹوٹ گیا۔ جہاز Java Sea میں گر چکا تھا۔ سوار تمام 189 لوگ جان سے گئے۔ ہم ان سب کو یاد کرتے ہیں۔ رپورٹس کے مطابق قریب ایک oil platform کے workers نے جہاز کو گرتے دیکھا۔ مگر cockpit میں آخر کیا ہو رہا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔

Magar sirf 3 minute baad captain ne controller se wapas airport aane ki ijazat mangi. Wajah thi flight-control ke masail. Phir 6:33 par air traffic control ka rabta toot gaya. Jahaz Java Sea mein gir chuka tha. Sawar tamam 189 log jaan se gaye. Hum in sab ko yaad karte hain. Reports ke mutabiq qareeb aik oil platform ke workers ne jahaz ko girte dekha. Magar cockpit mein aakhir kya ho raha tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.titleEn: Why Boeing Built MCAS: The Shortcut Behind Two Crashes
shorts.text: ایک چھوٹا سا software، اور 346 جانیں۔ اس کا نام تھا MCAS۔ مگر Boeing نے اسے بنایا کیوں؟ دوستو، کہانی شروع ہوتی ہے engines سے۔ 737 MAX کے LEAP engines پچھلی generations سے بڑے تھے۔ اس لیے انہیں wing کے آگے اور زمین سے زیادہ اونچائی پر لگانا پڑا۔ اس سے جہاز کی aerodynamics بدل گئی۔ flaps up، high angle of attack اور manual flight میں جہاز کی ناک اوپر اٹھنے کی طرف مائل ہو جاتی تھی۔ Boeing چاہتا تھا کہ MAX بالکل پرانے 737 Next Generation جیسا محسوس ہو۔ یوں دونوں ایک ہی type rating share کر سکتے تھے۔ Boeing نے کہا کہ simulator training کی ضرورت نہیں رہی۔ لیکن اس بچت کی قیمت کیا نکلی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Aik chota sa software, aur 346 jaanein. Is ka naam tha MCAS. Magar Boeing ne ise banaya kyun? Dosto, kahani shuru hoti hai engines se. 737 MAX ke LEAP engines pichli generations se bare thay. Is liye unhein wing ke aage aur zameen se zyada oonchai par lagana para. Is se jahaz ki aerodynamics badal gayi. flaps up, high angle of attack aur manual flight mein jahaz ki naak oopar uthne ki taraf mail ho jati thi. Boeing chahta tha ke MAX bilkul purane 737 Next Generation jaisa mehsoos ho. Yun dono aik hi type rating share kar sakte thay. Boeing ne kaha ke simulator training ki zaroorat nahi rahi. Lekin is bachat ki qeemat kya nikli? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Boeing's larger LEAP engines changed how the 737 MAX handled, and MCAS was added to make it feel like the older 737.
Why a cost-saving idea became a safety question.

shorts.hook: Pehle hi ghanti baj chuki thi
shorts.text: حادثے سے پہلے ہی خطرے کی گھنٹی بج چکی تھی۔ NTSC نے 7 November کو تصدیق کی کہ آخری سے تیسری اور چوتھی flight پر AoA sensors کے مسائل آئے تھے۔ Bali میں engineers نے سوچا کہ sensor بدلنے سے مسئلہ حل ہو جائے گا۔ چنانچہ ایک AoA sensor بدل دیا گیا۔ یہ replacement sensor ایک used پرزہ تھا، جو امریکی کمپنی Xtra Aerospace نے فراہم کیا۔ بعد کی تحقیقات میں پتا چلا کہ بھیجتے وقت ہی یہ شاید miscalibrated تھا۔ پھر Denpasar سے Jakarta کی flight میں جہاز نے اچانک غوطہ لگایا۔ اس flight کے crew نے inflight procedures پر عمل کیا اور جہاز safely اتار لیا۔ تو اگلی صبح کیا ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Hadse se pehle hi khatre ki ghanti baj chuki thi. NTSC ne 7 November ko tasdeeq ki ke aakhri se teesri aur chauthi flight par AoA sensors ke masail aaye thay. Bali mein engineers ne socha ke sensor badalne se masla hal ho jaye ga. Chunancha aik AoA sensor badal diya gaya. Yeh replacement sensor aik used purza tha, jo American company Xtra Aerospace ne faraham kiya. Baad ki tehqeeqat mein pata chala ke bhejte waqt hi yeh shayad miscalibrated tha. Phir Denpasar se Jakarta ki flight mein jahaz ne achanak ghota lagaya. Is flight ke crew ne inflight procedures par amal kiya aur jahaz safely utar liya. To agli subah kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
